LunchDash sat idle for twenty minutes and then answered an 11:00 tap instantly. A classmate says it must have been ""stuck on line 200"" waiting to continue. What does the CED say is actually going on?
Incorrect. Twenty minutes of invisible work is the sequential picture the case is designed to rule out.
Incorrect. Sequential flow has no mechanism for skipping ahead on demand. The instant response is the signature of event-driven execution.
<div id=""chk-1-fb-C"" class=""mcq-feedback correct-fb"">Correct. This is the CED distinction exactly. The order-handling code has no place ""in line"" that the program works toward
column2: it ran because the tap event fired.

column1: Incorrect. Nothing in the log describes the operating system suspending anything, and the CED explains the behaviour without needing it.
At 10:30 the cafeteria inventory software transmitted ""pizza: 0 remaining"" and the tile turned gray. No human touched the app. Was that input?
Incorrect. Typing and tapping are two input forms among several. The form does not decide whether something counts as input.
Correct. Software-to-software input is completely normal. Data was sent to the computer for processing by the program, which is the CED definition of input.
Incorrect. The earlier configuration is not the input. The transmitted data is, and it arrived from another program.
Incorrect. The humans-only assumption is exactly what this row exists to break. The CED allows other programs as an input source.
Two students tapped the same ""Surprise me"" button seconds apart and were offered different meals. One files a bug report saying the program is broken. What is the correct ruling?
Correct. The inputs matched, but each student's remembered internal values differed, so the same tap legitimately computes a different offer.
Incorrect. Calling it random without naming prior state is the incomplete answer. Nothing here violates a rule the CED states.
Incorrect. Timing is not the difference that matters. Two identical taps would still differ in outcome because the stored state differs.
Incorrect. That rule would be true only if input were the only thing output could depend on. The CED explicitly allows prior state as well.
The nine lines inside LunchDash that gray out a sold-out tile: what is the precise CED term for them?
Incorrect. Behavior is how the program functions during execution, described from the user side, not the lines themselves.
Incorrect. The arriving data is the event. The lines that respond to it are code.
Incorrect. A program is the whole collection that performs a task when run. These nine lines cannot stand alone.
Correct. The part versus whole distinction is the entire point of the term. A code segment is part of a program.
One tap on the pizza tile produced a confirmation on screen and a buzz. How many outputs is that, and in what forms?
Incorrect. The vibration motor is a different device from the display, and a buzz is tactile rather than visual.
Incorrect. Output is any data sent from a program to a device. The buzz qualifies, so this undercounts.
Correct. One input can legitimately produce several outputs, and here they arrive in two different forms on two different devices.
Incorrect. This drops the confirmation, which is just as much an output as the buzz.
ENRICHMENT: during the quiet twenty minutes LunchDash looked like it was running no code at all, yet it answered instantly. What distinguishes an idle app from a frozen one?

column2: frozen means too many arrived at once</button>
frozen means a full queue with the loop blocked</button>
frozen means it is still loaded but unresponsive</button>

column1: Incorrect. Volume is not the distinction. A frozen app is blocked by a handler that will not return, whatever the queue depth.
Correct. The event loop never stopped during the idle window, which is exactly why the tap was dispatched on its very next pass.
Incorrect. An exited program cannot answer a tap instantly twenty minutes later.
Incorrect. They are opposite failures. One is healthy waiting, the other is a handler hogging the loop and never returning control.

7 questions on the same ideas, drawn from this exercise's answer key. These are auto-graded and reported.
Trace 1: a pedestrian presses the metal crosswalk button. Name the input precisely.
Incorrect. The chirp is an output the press causes. It is not the input.
Incorrect. The controller is the program receiving the input, not a source sending text to itself.
Incorrect. Nothing is seen by the program here, and no other program supplied the press.
Correct. A press is a physical action by a person, and it is an event: a defined action that supplies input data to the program.
Trace 1: one press lights the WALK symbol and plays a chirp. Count and classify the outputs.
Incorrect. The background cycle is separate. The press produced new data sent to devices.
Incorrect. The count follows the data sent to devices, not the number of inputs that caused it.
Correct. One input, two outputs, two forms, two devices. That pairing is what the trace has to name.
Incorrect. A chirp is audio and reaches a speaker, which is a different device from the display.
Trace 1: is the crosswalk controller sequential or event-driven?
Incorrect. The cycle keeps running between presses, so not everything waits on the button.
Correct. Naming the hybrid is what a complete ruling requires. Both models are present and they govern different parts.
Incorrect. The controller runs a program, which is what makes the execution-model question meaningful.
Incorrect. That describes the background cycle and misses the pedestrian feature entirely.
Trace 2: at 2:00 a.m. the portal emails summaries to families. Nothing appears on any screen and nobody is awake. Did the program produce output?
Correct. This is the trap the trace is built around, and the rule settles it cleanly.
Incorrect. The output happened when the program sent it. A recipient opening it later is not what makes it output.
Incorrect. Nobody needs to be watching. The definition turns on data leaving the program for a device.
Incorrect. The delivery mechanism does not change what it is. Data went from the program to mail servers and on to devices.
Trace 2: the district gradebook software transmits grades to the portal with no person involved. What is the input source?

column2: the portal reads its own database</button>

column1: Incorrect. Earlier human data entry is not the input to this program at this moment. The transmission is.
Incorrect. Data crossed the program boundary inbound, which is what makes it input rather than a self-contained read.
Incorrect. The mail server is an output destination, not the source of the incoming data.
Correct. Software-to-software input is ordinary, and naming it is what the trace requires.
Trace 3: the same raccoon triggers the doorbell at 2 a.m. and at 2 p.m., but only the night visit turns on the spotlight. What explains the difference?
Incorrect. Treating the setting as an input is the tempting misread. It was not supplied by the event.
Incorrect. The event is the same motion detection either way. What differs is what the program remembers.
Correct. A setting chosen hours earlier is invisible in the moment and decisive for the output, which is the textbook internal value.
Incorrect. Nothing random is involved. The behaviour is fully explained by input plus stored state.

column2: both built combo multipliers during play. How do those two remembered values differ?

column1: Incorrect. The server delivered song data. Neither remembered value arrived with it.
Correct. Same rule, two different lifetimes, and distinguishing them is what a complete challenge-level answer shows.
Incorrect. The taps alone cannot explain different scores from identical patterns. Stored values are doing the work.
Incorrect. The multiplier is not supplied from outside the program. The program itself wrote it.
